articleTitle: Microstrip compensation of fibre chromatic dispersion in optically amplified coherent systems
abstract: The authors have been investigating the effectiveness of dispersion compensation techniques implemented at the microwave intermediate frequency of a heterodyne coherent detection receiver. This builds upon and develops further preliminary ideas proposed to date for single span systems in which the total chromatic dispersion of the fibre is relatively modest. Specifically, they have investigated theoretically and experimentally the effectiveness for chromatic dispersion compensation of dispersive microstrip structures which shall be discussed later.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microwave frequency operation of a low-voltage InGaAs/InP multiple-quantum-well reflective Fabry-Perot modulator
abstract: Useful modulation at frequencies in excess of 1.3 GHz has been achieved in a long-wavelength InGaAs/InP multiple-quantum-well reflective modulator. Microwave frequency operation of the modulator was investigated using a free-space link, is shown schematically. The modulator was illuminated with focussed radiation from a Fabry-Perot laser emitting close to the 1610 nm resonance, use of a polarisation-selective beam splitter in conjunction with a quarter-wave retarder providing efficient resolution of power reflected from the device in the presence of stray power from other system components. RF drive to the modulator via a bias network permitted investigation of behaviour under a variety of bias conditions. Reflected modulated power was detected using a reverse biased pin photodiode, again coupled via a bias network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Describes an edge-coupled p-i-n photodiode that is monolithically integrated with a 1.5 mu m optical preamplifier. This device not only compensates for coupling loss, but also provides net gain. The frequency response of two devices of photodiode lengths of 35 mu m and 75 mu m were measured. The bandwidth measured were 15 and 35 GHz, and the gain were 10 dB and 6 dB respectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microstrip and coplanar design considerations for microwave bandwidth PIN-HEMT optical receivers
abstract: Optical fibre systems which operate in the multi-Gbit/s regime or utilise microwave subcarriers require low noise receivers with bandwidths spanning many GHz. Such receivers may be realised with hybrid circuits using discrete devices mounted on microstrip or coplanar substrates. The paper shows that the microstrip approach takes advantage of a broad library of well established CAD models, however certain difficulties can arise in the practical realisation of receivers. These difficulties are avoided in the coplanar approach, which generally realises a broader bandwidth, but CAD models are less well developed. In either case it is shown that a simple hybrid construction may be used to produce high performance optical receivers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 1*32 polarisation independent switch for analogue systems
abstract: The authors present results on a 1*32 polarisation independent optical switch, using a recently developed optical switch cell which allows fabrication tolerant, high complexity matrices to be fabricated, whilst providing low drive circuit complexity. They also outline their application in microwave signal processing systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Direct optimisation and realisation of microstrip signal shaping networks for multi-gigabit optical communication
abstract: Describes a design technique for the direct optimisation of distributed post-detection filters, realised in microstrip, for multi-gigabit optical receivers. The authors consider initially ideal, lossless transmission line structures before extending the concept to practical microstrip structures. Microstrip is an appropriate medium for implementation since it is a mature, well-understood technology that allows easy integration of the filter with the other receiver signal processing operations via hybrid structures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dispersive considerations in microwave optical systems
abstract: The dispersive mechanism which limits the transmission of microwave signals through step index singlemode (SISM) fibre at 1550 nm is outlined. Consideration of differential phase offsets in the optical field as it propagates through a dispersive fibre is shown to result in periodic conversion of an amplitude modulated (AM) signal into a frequency modulated (FM) signal which can not be recovered by direct detection. This effect is shown to be significant at frequencies in excess of 10 GHz after just a few tens of kilometres of SISM fibre.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Equalisation of high bandwidth optical systems by phase reversal modulators
abstract: Constant group delay and well behaved magnitude response are important characteristics of broadband communications systems. Conventionally, electronic equalisers are employed to mitigate the effect of signal distortion introduced by nonideal components within the system. However, over wide bandwidths electronic equalisation (or pulse shaping) is problematic. The authors propose a method of equalising the system response optically, by employing group-delay compensating external modulators with phase reversal electrodes. These devices may allow the construction of higher data rate systems. They demonstrate the principle by equalising the response of a 14 GHz photodiode.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical beam-former for microwave phased array antennas
abstract: Presents a new beam forming technique for use in optically controlled phased array antennas. The system uses two optical fibre networks to produce a beam having independently specified frequency and aperture phase slope. The theory of the system is presented together with a description of the experimental implementation and results for a system operating at L-band.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diode laser bandwidth optimisation for analogue application
abstract: The authors have defined a damping factor, zeta , which directly indicates the level of damping on the frequency response of a laser diode. In order to optimize the laser intrinsic bandwidth for an analogue lightwave system, zeta has to be 0.707; and this value of zeta is different from that of an optimal performance digital system which normally requires zeta >1. They have also found an approximate expression for the maximum possible bandwidth, BW/sub max/, and its corresponding biasing current, I/sub max/, in terms of the device parameters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A lithium niobate bandpass modulator for optical subcarrier transmission systems
abstract: A novel lithium niobate bandpass optical modulator with a three section phase reversal travelling wave coded electrode structure has been developed for optical fibre system applications. The device exhibited a switching voltage of 8.5 V at a peak response of 11.2 GHz, and an upper and lower-3 dB optical modulation response of 15 GHz and 7.1 GHz, respectively. The results obtained agreed closely with theoretical models of the modulation response of coded electrode devices. A new packaging technology has been developed which allows the bandpass modulator to be housed in a fully hermetic environment without deteriorating its intrinsic high speed performance. For applications in the 11 GHz to 14 GHz band initial studies indicate that bandpass lithium niobate modulators are superior to conventional broadband lithium niobate modulators as a result of a lower required switching voltage and therefore lower required RF drive power.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A high speed laser package for optical communications
abstract: Describes work which is currently being undertaken at British Telecom Research Laboratories (BTRL) in response to the demand for a highspeed laser package for a variety of system applications. At present, commercial packages are limited in bandwidth to a few gigahertz, whereas laser chips have been reported to at least 18 GHz. In order to evaluate these higher speed chips a test fixture is required, and for use in real systems, a package which meets practical electrical, optical, thermal, mechanical, and environmental conditions must be developed. A test fixture designed for laser chip assessment, and a package developed to host the laser and associated components are described, along with results obtained. The problems of intrapackage connection and interfacing are also addressed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An integrated optic 'mixer' for RF applications
abstract: Reports on some experiments which show how a Mach-Zehnder integrated optic modulator (IOM) can be used as an electro-optical signal processing component, whose operation is similar to that of a mixer in an RF system. This 'mixer' has been used in conjunction with an electronic frequency sweeper and a low pass optical detector to analyse the spectrum of an RF signal modulated on an optical carrier, whilst the signal is still in the optical domain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical clock generation and carrier extraction techniques using 790 nm self-pulsating laser diodes
abstract: Self-pulsating laser diodes (SP-LD) emitting at 790 nm wavelength have found widespread application as low-noise, low-cost optical sources in compact disc (CD) systems. The requisite immunity to reflection-induced noise is obtained by gigahertz frequency self-pulsation of the laser emission coupled with significant chirping of each Fabry-Perot mode. It is the resultant low-coherence of the optical output which reduces CD reflection noise. Subsequent work has shown that the SP-LD characteristics as described by Poh (1985) predict a pronounced modulation transfer function nonlinearity at the self-pulsation frequency and also well-defined injection-locking behaviour. These effects are exploited in the experimental work described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multivariate optimisation criteria for microwave subcarrier PSK optical transmission systems
abstract: Describes a multivariate analysis technique for M-ary PSK direct detection subcarrier broadcast optical networks. The optimum modulation index, avalanche photodiode gain and number of levels M may all be determined at the planning stage. Additionally, maximum permissible relative intensity noise may be assessed. Allowable network distribution loss is then specified by the resultant receiver sensitivity. In a five channel example, a 4-PSK format was seen to have a small sensitivity advantage compared to 2-PSK. The 8-and 16- PSK schemes both introduce penalties compared to 2-PSK.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 2.488 Gbit/s FSK field demonstration over a 132 km submarine cable employing an erbium power amplifier
abstract: The authors used FSK modulation and optical delay demodulation to demonstrate a sixteen-fold upgrade capability for the UK-Channel Islands No. 7 submarine cable, achieving a line-rate of 2.488 Gbit/s over 132 km nondispersion shifted fibre. Erbium power amplifiers were used to provide a generous operating margin of approximately=10 dB and the compact spectrum of FSK modulation overcame the dispersion penalty that would have resulted from direct modulation. Further laboratory measurements have shown that transmission at 5 Gbit/s over 150 km nondispersion shifted fibre, equivalent to 2.5 Gbit/s over 600 km, is possible without any significant dispersion penalty. Numerical simulations broadly substantiate these measurements and further predict that transmission over greater than 1000 km is feasible, given that the fibre loss is overcome through the use of optical amplifiers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
